title: CAM (Content-Addressable Memory)
summary: CAM (Content-Addressable Memory) is a special memory that searches all entries in parallel for a match. Each cell is an SRAM cell with a comparison circuit (XNOR + match line). On a search, the search key is broadcast to all rows; matching rows pull their match line low. Priority encoder selects the highest-priority match. Used in TLBs, caches (tag lookup), and network routers (forwarding tables).

structure.meaning: SRAM cell (6T) + comparison circuit (2-4 transistors: XNOR + pass transistor).
Broadcast to all rows in parallel.
Precharged high; pulled low if any bit mismatches.
Indicates if the entry is valid (not empty).
Ternary CAM (TCAM): each bit can be 0, 1, or don't-care (X). Used for IP routing (subnet masks).

notes: CAM is O(1) search (vs O(n) for RAM).
TCAM (Ternary CAM) supports don't-care bits (for subnet matching).
CAM is used in TLBs (fast address translation), cache tag lookup, and network routers.
CAM is expensive (area and power): 9-10 transistors per bit vs 1 for DRAM.
CAM search is parallel (all rows simultaneously).
